claim: Post-translational control of PERIOD stability by Casein Kinase 1δ and ε (CK1) plays a key regulatory role in metazoan circadian rhythms.
source: Post-translational control of PERIOD stability by Casein Kinase 1δ and ε (CK1) plays a key regulatory role in metazoan circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about CK1's role in circadian rhythms, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A molecular switch involving a highly conserved anion binding site in CK1 controls conformation of the kinase activation loop.
source: Here we describe a molecular switch involving a highly conserved anion binding site in CK1. This switch controls conformation of the kinase activation loop and determines which sites on mammalian PER2 are preferentially phosphorylated, thereby directly regulating PER2 stability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by crystallographic and molecular dynamics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The activation loop switch determines which sites on mammalian PER2 are preferentially phosphorylated.
source: This switch controls conformation of the kinase activation loop and determines which sites on mammalian PER2 are preferentially phosphorylated, thereby directly regulating PER2 stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinase assays showing differential phosphorylation of FASP and Degron sites.

claim: The activation loop switch directly regulates PER2 stability.
source: This switch controls conformation of the kinase activation loop and determines which sites on mammalian PER2 are preferentially phosphorylated, thereby directly regulating PER2 stability.
evidence: This is supported by PER2::LUC half-life measurements showing changes in stability with different kinase mutants.

claim: Period-altering kinase mutations from humans to Drosophila differentially modulate the activation loop switch.
source: We show that period-altering kinase mutations from humans to Drosophila differentially modulate this activation loop switch to elicit predictable changes in PER2 stability, providing a foundation to understand and further manipulate CK1 regulation of circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on multiple kinase mutants and their effects on PER2 phosphorylation and stability.

claim: Period-altering kinase mutations elicit predictable changes in PER2 stability.
source: We show that period-altering kinase mutations from humans to Drosophila differentially modulate this activation loop switch to elicit predictable changes in PER2 stability, providing a foundation to understand and further manipulate CK1 regulation of circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between FASP/Degron enzyme efficiency ratios and PER2::LUC half-life.

claim: Circadian rhythms are generated by a set of interlocked transcription/translation feedback loops that elicit daily oscillations in gene expression.
source: Circadian rhythms are generated by a set of interlocked transcription/translation feedback loops that elicit daily oscillations in gene expression to confer temporal regulation to behavior, metabolism, DNA repair and more (Bass and Lazar, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: PERIOD proteins nucleate assembly of large, multimeric complexes with CRY1 and CRY2.
source: The PERIOD proteins (PER1 and PER2) nucleate assembly of large, multimeric complexes with the circadian repressors CRY1 and CRY2 that directly bind to and inhibit the core circadian transcription factor, CLOCK:BMAL1, on a daily basis (Aryal et al., 2017; Michael et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER-CRY complexes directly bind to and inhibit CLOCK:BMAL1 on a daily basis.
source: The PERIOD proteins (PER1 and PER2) nucleate assembly of large, multimeric complexes with the circadian repressors CRY1 and CRY2 that directly bind to and inhibit the core circadian transcription factor, CLOCK:BMAL1, on a daily basis (Aryal et al., 2017; Michael et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PERs are stoichiometrically limiting for the assembly of essential repressive complexes.
source: PERs are stoichiometrically limiting for the assembly of these essential repressive complexes (Lee et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CK1δ and CK1ε remain stably anchored to PER1 and PER2 throughout the circadian cycle.
source: These clock-associated kinases are somewhat unusual, in that they remain stably anchored to PER1 and PER2 throughout the circadian cycle (Aryal et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2001) via a conserved Casein Kinase Binding Domain (CKBD) (Eide et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CK1 kinases anchor to PER proteins via a conserved Casein Kinase Binding Domain (CKBD).
source: These clock-associated kinases are somewhat unusual, in that they remain stably anchored to PER1 and PER2 throughout the circadian cycle (Aryal et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2001) via a conserved Casein Kinase Binding Domain (CKBD) (Eide et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in CK1δ/ε exert powerful control over circadian period, altering the intrinsic timing of circadian rhythms by hours in vivo.
source: Mutations in CK1δ/ε (hereafter referred to jointly as CK1), as well as PER2, exert powerful control over circadian period, altering the intrinsic timing of circadian rhythms by hours in vivo (Lowrey et al., 2000; Toh et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in PER2 exert powerful control over circadian period, altering the intrinsic timing of circadian rhythms by hours in vivo.
source: Mutations in CK1δ/ε (hereafter referred to jointly as CK1), as well as PER2, exert powerful control over circadian period, altering the intrinsic timing of circadian rhythms by hours in vivo (Lowrey et al., 2000; Toh et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circadian period is linked to the timing of sleep onset.
source: Because circadian period is linked to the timing of sleep onset, PER2 or CK1-dependent alterations to human circadian period manifest as sleep phase disorders that influence behavior and wellbeing on a daily basis (Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PER2 or CK1-dependent alterations to human circadian period manifest as sleep phase disorders.
source: Because circadian period is linked to the timing of sleep onset, PER2 or CK1-dependent alterations to human circadian period manifest as sleep phase disorders that influence behavior and wellbeing on a daily basis (Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PER2 is regulated by a CK1-dependent phosphoswitch where kinase activity at two antagonistic sites functionally interact to control PER2 stability.
source: PER2 is regulated by a CK1-dependent phosphoswitch, where kinase activity at two antagonistic sites functionally interact to control PER2 stability (Masuda et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Degradation of PER2 is initiated by phosphorylation of a Degron located several hundred residues upstream of the CKBD to recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase, β-TrCP.
source: Two features define the CK1 phosphoswitch: degradation is initiated by phosphorylation of a Degron located several hundred residues upstream of the CKBD to recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase, β-TrCP (Eide et al., 2005; Vanselow et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PER2 degradation is counteracted by sequential phosphorylation of five serines embedded within the CKBD known as the FASP region.
source: this is counteracted by sequential phosphorylation of five serines embedded within the CBKD known as the FASP region (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The FASP region is named for a Ser to Gly polymorphism in human PER2 that disrupts stabilizing multi-site phosphorylation, shortens circadian period, and leads to Familial Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome.
source: This region is named for a Ser to Gly polymorphism in human PER2 that disrupts this stabilizing multi-site phosphorylation, shortens circadian period, and leads to Familial Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome (Toh et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutation of the Degron phosphorylation site stabilizes PER2 to significantly compromise circadian rhythms.
source: Mutation of the Degron phosphorylation site has the opposite effect, stabilizing PER2 to significantly compromise circadian rhythms (Reischl et al., 2007) in a manner similar to its constitutive overexpression (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The balance of stabilizing and degrading phosphorylation by CK1 leads to a complex temporal pattern of degradation in PER2 that is important for circadian timing.
source: Therefore, the balance of stabilizing and degrading phosphorylation by CK1 leads to a complex temporal pattern of degradation in PER2 that is important for circadian timing (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CK1 is important for circadian timing in eukaryotic organisms from humans to Drosophila, Neurospora, and green algae.
source: Despite the importance of CK1 for circadian timing in eukaryotic organisms from humans to Drosophila, Neurospora, and green algae (Görl et al., 2001; Kloss et al., 1998; van Ooijen et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2005), little is known about how its activity is regulated on clock protein substrates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CK1 is thought of as an anion- or phosphate-directed kinase, relying on negative charge on the substrate to template activity in the pSxxS consensus motif.
source: CK1 is thought of as an anion- or phosphate-directed kinase, relying on negative charge on the substrate to template activity in the pSxxS consensus motif (Flotow et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Biochemical studies exploring CK1 activity have primarily relied on the non-physiological acidic substrates casein and phosvitin.
source: Consistent with this, biochemical studies exploring CK1 activity have primarily relied on the non-physiological acidic substrates casein (Venerando et al., 2014) and phosvitin (Lowrey et al., 2000), or used peptides harboring anion- or phosphate-driven motifs (Isojima et al., 2009; Marin et al., 1994; Shinohara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro studies of clock-relevant kinase mutants using non-physiological substrates have led to the conclusion that CK1 mutants that either decrease or increase period length all have reduced kinase activity.
source: However, in vitro studies of clock-relevant kinase mutants using these non-physiological substrates have led to the puzzling conclusion that CK1 mutants that either decrease or increase period length all have reduced kinase activity (Kivimäe et al., 2008; Venkatesan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CK1ε tau allele markedly speeds up the clock, leading to a ~ 20 hr period.
source: The importance of anion binding is highlighted by the CK1ε tau allele that markedly speeds up the clock, leading to a ~ 20 hr period (Lowrey et al., 2000; Ralph and Menaker, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The R178C mutation in tau alters a phosphate binding pocket on the surface of the kinase to block the ability of CK1 to further phosphorylate primed or acidic substrates.
source: The R178C mutation in tau alters a phosphate binding pocket on the surface of the kinase to block the ability of CK1 to further phosphorylate primed or acidic substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tau has reduced activity on the FASP region in vitro.
source: We discovered that tau has reduced activity on the FASP region in vitro, but exhibits a gain of function on the Degron site.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tau exhibits a gain of function on the Degron site.
source: We discovered that tau has reduced activity on the FASP region in vitro, but exhibits a gain of function on the Degron site.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The tau allele inverts substrate selectivity on PER2 relative to the wild-type kinase to promote PER2 degradation.
source: Therefore, the tau allele inverts substrate selectivity on PER2 relative to the wild-type kinase to promote PER2 degradation.
evidence: This is supported by the combined data on FASP and Degron phosphorylation.

claim: The crystal structure of the tau kinase domain revealed the presence of a two-state conformational switch in the CK1 activation loop.
source: A mechanism for inverted substrate selectivity was suggested by the crystal structure of the tau kinase domain, which revealed the presence of a two-state conformational switch in the CK1 activation loop.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anion binding near the activation loop biases the switch towards a conformation that favors the FASP substrate.
source: Anion binding near the activation loop biases the switch towards a conformation that favors the FASP substrate, while mutations that disfavor anion binding enhance activity towards the Degron.
evidence: This is supported by structural and kinase assay data.

claim: Mutations that disfavor anion binding enhance activity towards the Degron.
source: Anion binding near the activation loop biases the switch towards a conformation that favors the FASP substrate, while mutations that disfavor anion binding enhance activity towards the Degron.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data on Site 2 mutants.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the alternate conformation is stabilized in tau.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the alternate conformation is stabilized in tau, forming the basis for its enhanced activity on the Degron.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The alternate activation loop conformation in tau forms the basis for its enhanced activity on the Degron.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the alternate conformation is stabilized in tau, forming the basis for its enhanced activity on the Degron.
evidence: This is an inference based on MD simulations and kinase assay data.

claim: Short period kinase mutants from Drosophila to humans differentially bias the activation loop switch to enhance phosphorylation of the Degron and turnover of PER2.
source: A comprehensive analysis of other short period kinase mutants from Drosophila to humans finds that they differentially bias this intrinsic switch to enhance phosphorylation of the Degron and turnover of PER2.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assays and PER2 stability measurements on multiple mutants.

claim: The anion-triggered activation loop switch may be a general mechanism regulating CK1 substrate selection.
source: Therefore, the anion-triggered activation loop switch may be a general mechanism regulating CK1 substrate selection.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: CK1 primes FASP phosphorylation in a slow, rate-limiting step at serine 659.
source: We recently demonstrated that CK1 primes FASP phosphorylation in a slow, rate-limiting step at serine 659 (mouse PER2 numbering, Figure 1A–B), with phosphorylation of the downstream consensus sites following rapidly in a sequential manner (dashed arrows at pSxxS consensus, Figure 1B) (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Phosphorylation of the downstream consensus sites in FASP follows rapidly in a sequential manner after priming at S659.
source: We recently demonstrated that CK1 primes FASP phosphorylation in a slow, rate-limiting step at serine 659 (mouse PER2 numbering, Figure 1A–B), with phosphorylation of the downstream consensus sites following rapidly in a sequential manner (dashed arrows at pSxxS consensus, Figure 1B) (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: R178 sits at Site 1, located adjacent to the active site.
source: R178 sits at Site 1, located adjacent to the active site, and has been postulated to bind a phosphorylated priming site to position the downstream serine of the consensus motif near the active site (Longenecker et al., 1996; Zeringo and Bellizzi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: R178 has been postulated to bind a phosphorylated priming site to position the downstream serine of the consensus motif near the active site.
source: R178 sits at Site 1, located adjacent to the active site, and has been postulated to bind a phosphorylated priming site to position the downstream serine of the consensus motif near the active site (Longenecker et al., 1996; Zeringo and Bellizzi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tau should preferentially disrupt phosphorylation of the downstream consensus sites in the FASP region due to its inability to recruit the primed substrate.
source: Based on this model, we predicted that tau should preferentially disrupt phosphorylation of the downstream consensus sites in the FASP region due to its inability to recruit the primed substrate.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural model.

claim: Tau had significantly lower activity than the WT kinase on primed FASP substrate.
source: As expected, tau had significantly lower activity than the WT kinase on this primed substrate (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Tau had significantly lower activity on the primed synthetic substrate CK1tide.
source: This was also true for a minimal, primed synthetic substrate CK1tide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation of the non-consensus priming site occurs with much slower kinetics than the downstream consensus sites.
source: As we observed before, phosphorylation of the non-consensus priming site occurs with much slower kinetics than the downstream consensus sites (Figure 1F–G) (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tau had significantly diminished activity on an unprimed FASP substrate.
source: To our surprise, we found that tau also had significantly diminished activity on an unprimed FASP substrate (Figure 1F–G), indicating that R178 is also important for the non-consensus priming event.
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: R178 is important for the non-consensus priming event at the FASP region.
source: To our surprise, we found that tau also had significantly diminished activity on an unprimed FASP substrate (Figure 1F–G), indicating that R178 is also important for the non-consensus priming event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinase assay data.

claim: The decrease in activity of tau on the priming site was validated using an ELISA-based kinase assay with an antibody specific for phosphorylated S659.
source: The decrease in activity of tau on the priming site was also validated using an ELISA-based kinase assay with an antibody that is specific for phosphorylated S659 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Priming is required to initiate phosphorylation of downstream sites in the FASP by CK1.
source: We established the requirement for priming to initiate phosphorylation of downstream sites in the FASP by CK1 (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The peaks for both pS659 and pS662 were decreased in volume for tau in the NMR kinase assay.
source: By contrast, we observed that the peaks for both pS659 and pS662 were decreased in volume for tau (Figure 1H–I), revealing that the ratio of consensus to priming activity (pS662/pS659) was similar in WT CK1 and tau (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: The ratio of consensus to priming activity (pS662/pS659) was similar in WT CK1 and tau.
source: By contrast, we observed that the peaks for both pS659 and pS662 were decreased in volume for tau (Figure 1H–I), revealing that the ratio of consensus to priming activity (pS662/pS659) was similar in WT CK1 and tau (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The activity of tau was much lower on the priming site at S659 relative to the WT kinase in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with our in vitro studies, the activity of tau was much lower on the priming site relative to the WT kinase (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Phosphorylation of S662 was decreased with tau in HEK293 cells.
source: As expected, phosphorylation of the subsequent serine was also decreased with tau (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The R178A mutant exhibited much lower activity on the FASP priming site in a cell-based assay.
source: To examine the possibility that loss of activity on the FASP region was specifically due to the cysteine mutation (R178C), we also tested an R178A mutant in the cell-based assay and found that it also exhibited much lower activity on the FASP priming site in a cell-based assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of R178 at the site one anion-binding pocket in tau leads to a reduction in both the slow priming step and the downstream sequential, primed phosphorylation of the FASP region.
source: Collectively, these data show that loss of R178 at the site one anion-binding pocket in tau leads to a reduction in both the slow priming step as well as the downstream sequential, primed phosphorylation of the FASP region.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the kinase assay data.

claim: Tau has increased activity on the Degron in HEK293 cells.
source: Using an antibody specific for phosphorylation of the CK1-dependent β-TrCP recruitment site at S478, we recapitulated the increased activity of tau on the Degron observed previously on myc-PER2 that was transiently expressed with the kinase in HEK293 cells (Figure 1L) (Gallego et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1L and a citation.

claim: WT kinase activity on the Degron increases with the S659A mutant that eliminates all phosphorylation of the FASP region.
source: Consistent with the phosphoswitch model that FASP phosphorylation antagonizes CK1 activity on the Degron (Figure 1A), we observed an increase in activity of WT kinase on the Degron with the S659A mutant that eliminates all phosphorylation of the FASP region (Figure 1L) (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1L and a citation.

claim: Tau has increased activity on the Degron in the S659A mutant.
source: We found that tau also had increased activity on the Degron in the S659A mutant, demonstrating that the tau mutant can still be regulated by the phosphoswitch.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data.

claim: Tau had significantly increased activity on the Degron peptide relative to WT kinase in vitro.
source: Here, we found that even on a peptide substrate in vitro, tau had significantly increased activity on the Degron relative to WT kinase (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: Both tau and WT kinase maintain their distinct substrate preference in the presence of both FASP and Degron peptides in vitro.
source: Moreover, both tau and WT kinase maintain their distinct substrate preference in the presence of both FASP and Degron peptides in vitro, with tau showing enhanced activity for the Degron relative to WT kinase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tau mutation leads to a fundamental change in CK1 activity and substrate specificity.
source: These data demonstrate that in addition to any regulation imparted by the phospho-FASP on the Degron in cells, the tau mutation leads to a fundamental change in CK1 activity and substrate specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined in vitro and cellular data.

claim: Both WT and tau coordinate an anion at Site three similarly.
source: Both WT and tau coordinate an anion at Site three similarly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tau mutation disrupted anion binding at Site 1.
source: However, the mutation disrupted anion binding at Site 1, although it led to only minor structural changes in this anion-binding pocket (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The tau mutation led to a loss of anion binding at Site two.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed a loss of anion binding at Site two in tau, mediated by an alternate conformation of the activation loop near this pocket that sterically blocks binding of the anion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The alternate conformation of the activation loop in tau initiates at G175, three residues upstream of the tau mutation.
source: This alternate conformation initiates at G175, three residues upstream of the tau mutation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A rotation of the backbone at G175 to a left-handed configuration dramatically alters the configuration of upstream residues to create a distinct conformation of the activation loop.
source: A rotation of the backbone at G175 to a left-handed configuration dramatically alters the configuration of upstream residues to create a distinct conformation of the activation loop (Figure 2D and ).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A backbone flip of a glycine at the conserved position G175 has been observed in other serine/threonine kinases, linking changes in conformation of the activation loop to regulation of kinase activity.
source: A backbone flip of a glycine at this conserved position has been observed in other serine/threonine kinases, linking changes in conformation of the activation loop to regulation of kinase activity (Nolen et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The 'loop up' conformation observed in tau may lead to different kinase activity than the 'loop down' conformation observed in the WT kinase.
source: therefore, the 'loop up' conformation observed in tau may lead to different kinase activity than the 'loop down' conformation observed in the WT kinase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Site 2 mutants (R127E, K154E, K171E) showed a modest decrease (~25%) in activity towards the FASP peptide.
source: We observed a modest decrease (~25%) in activity towards the FASP peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'loop down' conformation that is enforced by anion binding at Site 2 may be important for FASP activity.
source: suggesting that the 'loop down' conformation that is enforced by anion binding at Site 2 may be important for FASP activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the kinase assay data.

claim: Site 2 mutants (R127E, K154E, K171E) all increased activity towards the Degron, with a ~ 50% gain in efficiency for R127E.
source: Strikingly, these mutants all increased activity towards the Degron, with a ~ 50% gain in efficiency for R127E (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The K171E mutant retains sulfate binding at Site 2 to some degree.
source: To further examine the role of K171 in regulation of anion binding, we solved a structure of the K171E mutant crystallized in high sulfate conditions and found a full complement of three anions bound (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that local flexibility in the activation loop allows it to retain sulfate binding at Site 2 to some degree.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anion binding at Site 2 correlates with substrate selectivity on the FASP and Degron peptides.
source: Overall, these data suggest that anion binding at Site 2 correlates with substrate selectivity on the FASP and Degron peptides.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinase assay data.

claim: The change in selectivity with Site 2 mutants in vitro makes them much more tau-like.
source: Notably, the change in selectivity with Site 2 mutants in vitro makes them much more tau-like (Figure 2H)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both tau and charge reversion mutants at Site 2 lead to decreased PER2 stability in cells.
source: consistent with a recent report that both tau and charge reversion mutants at Site 2 lead to decreased PER2 stability in cells (Shinohara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Two copies of the kinase are found in the asymmetric unit of the tau crystal.
source: Two copies of the kinase are found in the asymmetric unit of the tau crystal.
evidence: This is a statement about the crystallographic data.

claim: The tau mutant kinase can take on either the 'loop down' or the 'loop up' conformation.
source: We discovered that the mutant kinase can take on either the 'loop down' or the 'loop up' conformation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The activation loop is not stabilized by crystal contacts in the alternate 'loop up' conformation.
source: The activation loop is not stabilized by crystal contacts in the alternate 'loop up' conformation and was explicitly modeled based on good density in both conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinase has an intrinsic ability to take on two discrete conformations in a switch-like manner.
source: suggesting that the kinase has an intrinsic ability to take on two discrete conformations in a switch-like manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystallographic data.

claim: Nearly all CK1 structures have been determined after crystallization with high concentrations of sulfate or citrate anions.
source: Since the first structure of CK1δ published in 1996, nearly all CK1 structures have been determined after crystallization with high concentrations of sulfate or citrate anions (Long et al., 2012; Longenecker et al., 1996; Minzel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prior crystallographic conditions have likely disfavored the alternate 'loop up' conformation.
source: Because anion binding at Site two is incompatible with the activation loop in its 'loop up' conformation, prior crystallographic conditions have likely disfavored this alternate conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The WT structure (PDB: 1CKJ) displays the same two discrete conformations marked by translocation of residue L173 in the activation loop.
source: Importantly, this structure also displays the same two discrete conformations marked by translocation of residue L173 in the activation loop (Figure 3A), confirming that this switch is an intrinsic property of the CK1δ kinase that has not been explored functionally.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The activation loop switch is an intrinsic property of the CK1δ kinase that has not been explored functionally.
source: Importantly, this structure also displays the same two discrete conformations marked by translocation of residue L173 in the activation loop (Figure 3A), confirming that this switch is an intrinsic property of the CK1δ kinase that has not been explored functionally.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crystallographic data.

claim: A survey of 68 chains from 26 different crystal structures of CK1δ demonstrated that tau and the WT kinase from PDB entry 1CKJ are the only structures of CK1δ to have ever been captured in the 'loop up' conformation.
source: A survey of 68 chains from 26 different crystal structures of CK1δ (in at least 7 space groups) demonstrated that tau and the WT kinase from PDB entry 1CKJ are the only structures of CK1δ to have ever been captured in the 'loop up' conformation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The residues that coordinate anion binding are broadly conserved in the CK1 family.
source: Moreover, the residues that coordinate anion binding are broadly conserved in the CK1 family and anions are also found bound in these sites in other CK1 family kinases (e.g., CK1ε, CK1ɣ3; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Anions are found bound in Sites 1, 2, and 3 in other CK1 family kinases.
source: Moreover, the residues that coordinate anion binding are broadly conserved in the CK1 family and anions are also found bound in these sites in other CK1 family kinases (e.g., CK1ε, CK1ɣ3; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by structural data referenced in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: A structure of anion-free CK1δ showed both conformations of the activation loop in the two molecules of the asymmetric unit.
source: To determine if we could independently capture the two states of the activation loop switch in the native kinase, we optimized sulfate-free crystallographic conditions and solved a structure of anion-free CK1δ. Similar to the 1CKJ structure, we observed both conformations of the activation loop in the two molecules of the asymmetric unit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CK1 has an anion-dependent switch in its activation loop.
source: Therefore, CK1 has an anion-dependent switch in its activation loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crystallographic data.

claim: The tau mutation appears to favor the 'loop up' conformation because it was observed in crystals that grew in the presence of high sulfate concentrations.
source: However, the tau mutation appears to favor the 'loop up' conformation because it was observed in crystals that grew in the presence of high sulfate concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystallographic data.

claim: The tau mutation allosterically regulates anion binding at Site 2 via the activation loop.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the tau mutation allosterically regulates anion binding at Site 2 via the activation loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and kinase assay data.

claim: The activation loop remained stably in position when simulations were started from the 'loop down' conformation for both tau and WT.
source: We found that the activation loop remained stably in position when simulations were started from the 'loop down' conformation for both tau and WT.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The 'loop down' conformation of the activation loop is intrinsically stable.
source: Similar results were seen when the anion was computationally removed from Site 2, suggesting that this conformation of the activation loop is intrinsically stable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In simulations starting from the 'loop up' conformation, the WT activation loop rapidly underwent a conformational change.
source: However, in simulations starting from the 'loop up' conformation, the WT activation loop rapidly underwent a conformational change, as shown by increased RMSDup values.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Conformational transitions from 'loop up' occurred more frequently in WT CK1 than in tau.
source: Importantly, these transitions occurred more frequently in WT CK1 than in tau (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The 'loop up' conformation is better tolerated in tau.
source: This confirms that the 'loop up' conformation is better tolerated in tau, consistent with our observation of this apparently rare conformation in our crystal structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MD simulation data.

claim: Y225 displayed more conformational freedom in tau compared to the WT kinase.
source: We also observed that Y225 displayed more conformational freedom in tau compared to the WT kinase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Y225 could be poised to coordinate the conformation of the activation loop with activity at Site 1.
source: Given that Y225 is directly adjacent to K224 in Site one and it also makes contact with L173 in the activation loop in its 'loop down' conformation, this suggests that Y225 could be poised to coordinate the conformation of the activation loop with activity at Site 1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural and MD simulation data.

claim: The 'loop down' conformation of the activation loop was accompanied by a strong disorganization of loop L-EF in tau.
source: However, we observed that the 'loop down' conformation of the activation loop was accompanied by a strong disorganization of loop L-EF in tau (Figure 4H), leading to significantly larger conformational freedom compared to the WT kinase (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: The disruption of Site one by loop L-EF dynamics in the tau mutation may be due to allosteric communication with the activation loop.
source: These data suggest that the disruption of Site one by loop L-EF dynamics in the tau mutation may be due to allosteric communication with the activation loop, and by proxy, anion binding at Site 2.
evidence: This is a speculation based on MD simulation data.

claim: Site two was completely open only when the activation loop was in the 'loop down' conformation for the WT kinase.
source: As expected, Site two was completely open only when the activation loop was in the 'loop down' conformation for the WT kinase (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Site 2 became partially open in simulations of the WT kinase starting from the 'loop up' conformation.
source: Interestingly, this site became partially open in simulations of the WT kinase starting from the 'loop up' conformation (Figure 4J), indicating that the intermediate conformational state observed in our simulations might allow the kinase to recover, to some extent, the ability to bind an anion at Site 2.
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4J.

claim: In WT, the substrate binding cleft was open more consistently with the activation loop in its preferred 'down' conformation.
source: In WT, the substrate binding cleft was open more consistently with the activation loop in its preferred 'down' conformation (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: The substrate binding cleft was open more consistently in tau in the 'loop up' conformation.
source: By contrast, the substrate binding cleft was open more consistently in tau in the 'loop up' conformation (Figure 4L)
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The substrate binding cleft often closed in tau when the activation loop was in the 'loop down' conformation due to the dynamic disordering of loop L-EF.
source: and, due to the dynamic disordering of loop L-EF, often closed when in the 'loop down' conformation (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by volumetric analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Closing of the substrate binding cleft in tau occurs due to the conformational disorganization in loop L-EF, which is allosterically induced when the activation loop is in the 'down' conformation.
source: Because the activation loop does not contact the substrate binding cleft, it cannot directly affect the shape of the cleft by steric effects. Instead, closing of the substrate binding cleft in tau occurs due to the conformational disorganization in loop L-EF, which is allosterically induced when the activation loop is in the 'down' conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MD simulation data.

claim: The 1st principal component consisted of a clear 'open-and-close' movement of the enzyme, achieved mainly by dislocation of the N-terminal lobe with respect to the top of helix F.
source: The 1st principal component consisted of a clear 'open-and-close' movement of the enzyme, achieved mainly by dislocation of the N-terminal lobe (N-lobe) with respect to the top of the helix F (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis of MD simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 'open-and-close' movement controls accessibility to the ATP-binding site and regulates substrate access in other kinases.
source: This mode of motion has been shown to control accessibility to the ATP-binding site and regulate substrate access in other kinases (McClendon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: WT CK1 sampled more of the open conformations compared to tau.
source: The histograms of the 1st principal component show that WT CK1 sampled more of the open conformations compared to tau (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 2nd principal component consisted of a twisting movement of the N-lobe with respect to the top of helix F and a significant rearrangement of loop L-EF.
source: The 2nd principal component consisted of a twisting movement of the N-lobe with respect to the top of helix F and a significant rearrangement of loop L-EF, which can either be extended or collapsed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When collapsed, loop L-EF had the effect of sterically closing the substrate binding cleft.
source: When collapsed, loop L-EF had the effect of sterically closing the substrate binding cleft.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA analysis.

claim: Loop L-EF adopts more extended conformations in WT CK1 and more collapsed conformations in tau.
source: The histograms of the 2nd PCA illustrate that loop L-EF adopts more extended conformations in WT CK1 and more collapsed conformations in tau (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The tau kinase never behaves fully like the WT enzyme.
source: Altogether, the GaMD simulations suggest that the tau kinase never behaves fully like the WT enzyme
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MD simulation data.

claim: Tau stabilizes the rare, Degron-preferring conformation of the activation loop that remodels the substrate binding cleft and excludes anion binding at Site 2.
source: compared to WT, it stabilizes the rare, Degron-preferring conformation of the activation loop that remodels the substrate binding cleft and excludes anion binding at Site 2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MD simulation and kinase assay data.

claim: When tau samples the 'loop down' conformation of the activation loop, it leads to a dynamic disordering of loop L-EF that favors conformations of the kinase that likely accounts for its decreased enzymatic efficiency on the FASP region.
source: By contrast, when tau samples the 'loop down' conformation of the activation loop, it leads to a dynamic disordering of loop L-EF that favors conformations of the kinase that likely accounts for its decrease enzymatic efficiency on the FASP region.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on MD simulation and kinase assay data.

claim: Doubletime (DBT) is the CK1δ/ε ortholog in Drosophila.
source: Doubletime (DBT), the CK1δ/ε ortholog in Drosophila, has one allele that causes a short circadian period (dbtS, P47S) while all others lead to a long period (Kloss et al., 1998; Rothenfluh et al., 2000; Suri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DBT has one allele (dbtS, P47S) that causes a short circadian period while all others lead to a long period.
source: Doubletime (DBT), the CK1δ/ε ortholog in Drosophila, has one allele that causes a short circadian period (dbtS, P47S) while all others lead to a long period (Kloss et al., 1998; Rothenfluh et al., 2000; Suri et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many long period mutations in DBT occur at or near catalytically important residues like the catalytic DFG motif and the regulatory spine that controls kinase activity.
source: Many long period mutations occur at or near catalytically important residues like the catalytic DFG motif and the regulatory spine that controls kinase activity (Figure 6B) (Taylor and Kornev, 2011; Muskus et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by structural mapping shown in Figure 6B and citations.

claim: Two loss of function alleles in DBT occur in the activation loop: dco18 (S181F) and dco2 (G175S).
source: Moreover, two loss of function alleles occur in the activation loop: dco18 (S181F) is located right behind the tau site (R178), linking it to the substrate binding channel and activation loop, while dco2 (G175S) occurs at the hinge point for the activation loop switch (Zilian et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Expressing mammalian CK1δ with the tau or dbtS mutation leads to short period circadian rhythms in flies.
source: In line with this, expressing mammalian CK1δ with the tau or dbts mutation leads to short period circadian rhythms in flies (Fan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The entire surface-exposed area linking Sites 1 and 2 and the substrate binding cleft are ≥95% identical in 20 species from humans to unicellular green alga where CK1 has been implicated in regulation of circadian clocks.
source: Consistent with this functional conservation, the entire surface-exposed area linking Sites 1 and 2 and the substrate binding cleft are ≥95% identical in 20 species from humans to unicellular green alga where CK1 has been implicated in regulation of circadian clocks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three short period mutants from humans and Drosophila (T44A, H46R, and P47S) colocalize in the N-lobe right above Site 2.
source: Three short period mutants from humans and Drosophila (T44A, H46R, and P47S) colocalize in the N-lobe right above Site 2 (Figure 6B) (Kloss et al., 1998; Brennan et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by structural mapping shown in Figure 6B and citations.

claim: The short period mutants T44A, H46R, and P47S each retained substantially more kinase activity on the FASP priming site than tau.
source: Similar to the Site two mutants we tested earlier (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the short period mutants T44A, H46R, and P47S each retained substantially more kinase activity on the FASP priming site than tau.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A triple mutant of T44A, H46R, and P47S (3M) did not have additive effects on FASP priming.
source: A triple mutant of all three short period mutants (3M) did not have additive effects.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The short period mutants T44A, H46R, and P47S retained kinase activity or exhibited modest increases in Degron phosphorylation relative to WT.
source: Likewise, they also appeared to retain kinase activity or even exhibited modest increases in Degron phosphorylation relative to WT (Figure 7B), although not to the same degree as tau.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mutants near Site two retain FASP priming activity while increasing activity at the Degron relative to WT.
source: On balance, it appears that mutants near Site two might act differently from tau in that they retain FASP priming activity while increasing activity at the Degron relative to WT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Western blot data.

claim: K224D retained FASP priming activity in HEK293 cells.
source: Unlike tau, K224D retained FASP priming activity in HEK293 cells (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: K224D exhibited a sharp increase in Degron phosphorylation similar to tau.
source: although it exhibited a sharp increase in Degron phosphorylation similar to tau (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The effect of K224D on FASP and Degron phosphorylation was not dependent on the charge inversion.
source: This effect was not dependent on the charge inversion, as we saw the same effect with a K224A mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enzyme efficiency of K224D was decreased on the FASP peptide.
source: Despite retaining priming activity in cells, we noticed that the enzyme efficiency of K224D was decreased on the FASP peptide, which contains multiple serines (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: K224D retained normal priming activity at S659 but phosphorylation of the downstream serines that conform to the pSxxS consensus motif was compromised relative to WT kinase.
source: Consistent with the cellular data, K224D retained normal priming activity at S659, but phosphorylation of the downstream serines that conform to the pSxxS consensus motif was compromised relative to WT kinase (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Tau reduces both priming and downstream phosphorylation of the FASP region.
source: Therefore, although tau and K224D both enhance Degron phosphorylation to a similar degree and lead to ~20 hr circadian periods (Lowrey et al., 2000; Shinohara et al., 2017), this is likely achieved through different mechanisms on the kinase—tau reduces both priming and downstream phosphorylation of the FASP region, while K224D (and K224A) likely just disrupts the phosphorylation of the downstream pSxxS consensus motifs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined NMR and Western blot data.

claim: K224D (and K224A) likely just disrupts the phosphorylation of the downstream pSxxS consensus motifs.
source: Therefore, although tau and K224D both enhance Degron phosphorylation to a similar degree and lead to ~20 hr circadian periods (Lowrey et al., 2000; Shinohara et al., 2017), this is likely achieved through different mechanisms on the kinase—tau reduces both priming and downstream phosphorylation of the FASP region, while K224D (and K224A) likely just disrupts the phosphorylation of the downstream pSxxS consensus motifs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined NMR and Western blot data.

claim: All of the CK1 mutants tested, apart from L173A, lead to a shorter half-life of PER2::LUC.
source: All of the mutants, apart from L173A, lead to a shorter half-life of PER2::LUC (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by PER2::LUC half-life measurements shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The L173A mutant substantially decreased kinase activity at both the FASP priming and Degron sites.
source: We found that the mutant substantially decreased kinase activity at both the FASP priming and Degron sites in the transfection-based assay and in vitro (Figure 7A–B and Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and kinase assay data.

claim: A double mutant of tau and L173A decreased activity on the Degron to a similar degree as L173A alone.
source: and a double mutant with tau decreased its activity on the Degron to a similar degree (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a significant correlation between PER2::LUC half-life and the intrinsic ratio of CK1 kinase activity on the FASP and Degron sites.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant correlation between PER2::LUC half-life and the intrinsic ratio of CK1 kinase activity on these two key sites that establish the phosphoswitch mechanism (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Activation loop dynamics orchestrate substrate specificity and contribute directly to the phosphoswitch regulation of PER2 stability.
source: Collectively, these data support a new model for CK1 regulation whereby activation loop dynamics orchestrate substrate specificity and contribute directly to the phosphoswitch regulation of PER2 stability, and therefore, the timing of circadian rhythms (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from the study.

claim: A conformational switch in the activation loop of CK1 regulates its activity on two regulatory regions in PER2 that control its stability and circadian timing in mammals.
source: We discovered a conformational switch in the activation loop of CK1 that regulates its activity on two regulatory regions in PER2 that control its stability and circadian timing in mammals (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Anion binding regulates the conformation of the activation loop switch to reshape the substrate binding cleft and thereby control substrate selectivity.
source: We show that anion binding regulates the conformation of this switch to reshape the substrate binding cleft and thereby control substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by structural and MD simulation data.

claim: All short period mutants in CK1 from Drosophila to mammals exhibit an intrinsic increase in kinase activity on the Degron.
source: Short period mutants in CK1 from Drosophila to mammals reveal that all exhibit an intrinsic increase in kinase activity on the Degron, consistent with an earlier observation in cells (Gallego et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data and a citation.

claim: The tau mutant disrupts the apparent allosteric regulation between anion binding sites.
source: However, the tau mutant disrupts the apparent allosteric regulation between anion binding sites
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural and MD simulation data.

claim: Tau alters the dynamics of the activation loop and adjacent loop L-EF that likely underlie the decreased activity of tau on the stabilizing FASP region.
source: our MD simulations revealed that tau alters the dynamics of the activation loop and adjacent loop L-EF that likely underlie the decreased activity of tau on the stabilizing FASP region.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: CK1 has remarkable, histone-like conservation (≥95% identity) of the entire surface-exposed area linking the two key anion binding sites and substrate binding cleft.
source: CK1 has remarkable, histone-like conservation (≥95% identity) of the entire surface-exposed area linking the two key anion binding sites and substrate binding cleft, suggesting that the mechanisms we discovered here likely apply broadly to circadian rhythms as well as other CK1-regulated processes in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The mechanisms discovered in this study likely apply broadly to circadian rhythms as well as other CK1-regulated processes in other eukaryotes.
source: CK1 has remarkable, histone-like conservation (≥95% identity) of the entire surface-exposed area linking the two key anion binding sites and substrate binding cleft, suggesting that the mechanisms we discovered here likely apply broadly to circadian rhythms as well as other CK1-regulated processes in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the conservation data.

claim: Binding of regulatory anions at conserved sites could arise from phosphorylated CK1 itself in cis via its autoinhibitory tail.
source: Binding of regulatory anions at these conserved sites could arise from phosphorylated CK1 itself in cis via its autoinhibitory tail (Rivers et al., 1998), or in trans from the binding of phosphorylated substrates like the FASP region, to allow for the generation of feedback regulation directly on the kinase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural findings and a citation.

claim: Binding of regulatory anions at conserved sites could arise in trans from the binding of phosphorylated substrates like the FASP region.
source: Binding of regulatory anions at these conserved sites could arise from phosphorylated CK1 itself in cis via its autoinhibitory tail (Rivers et al., 1998), or in trans from the binding of phosphorylated substrates like the FASP region, to allow for the generation of feedback regulation directly on the kinase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural findings.

claim: Changes in the sequence or phosphorylation of the autoinhibitory tail of CK1δ/ε could alter the balance of PER2 phosphorylation at the FASP or Degron to control circadian period.
source: In line with this, changes in the sequence (Fustin et al., 2018) or phosphorylation (Eng et al., 2017; Takano et al., 2004) of the autoinhibitory tail of CK1δ/ε could alter the balance of PER2 phosphorylation at the FASP or Degron to control circadian period.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dynamics of CK1δ/ε directly encode its activity in the PER2 phosphoswitch.
source: Therefore, our study demonstrates that the dynamics of CK1δ/ε directly encode its activity in the PER2 phosphoswitch (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from the study.

claim: The conformational equilibrium of the activation loop may play a role in the temperature-compensated activity of CK1δ/ε observed in vitro.
source: The conformational equilibrium of the activation loop may also play a role in the temperature-compensated activity of CK1δ/ε observed in vitro that is linked to loop L-EF, an insertion in the clock-relevant kinases CK1δ and CK1ε that plays a role in maintaining its relative insensitivity to temperature (Shinohara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and a citation.

claim: PER proteins have a special role in the mammalian clock as state variables that define both the timing and phase of circadian rhythms through changes in their abundance.
source: PER proteins seem to have a special role in the mammalian clock as state variables that define both the timing and phase of circadian rhythms through changes in their abundance (Balsalobre et al., 2000; Zylka et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CK1-dependent changes in PER abundance likely affect circadian period based on their role as stoichiometrically limiting factors in the assembly of transcriptional repressive complexes.
source: CK1-dependent changes in PER abundance likely affect circadian period based on their role as stoichiometrically limiting factors in the assembly of transcriptional repressive complexes in the feedback loop of the molecular clock (Aryal et al., 2017; Kim and Forger, 2012; Lee et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CK1 may target other clock proteins for phosphorylation in the repressive complexes.
source: Recent studies have shown that CK1 may allow target other clock proteins for phosphorylation in the repressive complexes (Aryal et al., 2017), a property that seems to be conserved in Drosophila (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many of the biologically important roles of CK1δ/ε and CK1ɑ depend on their activity at non-consensus sites.
source: However, we find it compelling that many of the biologically important roles of CK1δ/ε and the related kinase CK1ɑ as key regulators of Wnt signaling (Marin et al., 2003), the DNA damage response (Knippschild et al., 1997), cell cycle (Penas et al., 2015), and circadian rhythms (Kloss et al., 1998; Lowrey et al., 2000) depend on their activity at non-consensus sites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of CK1 kinases to phosphorylate lower affinity, non-consensus sites on PER2 is likely dependent on the formation of a stable, stoichiometric complex with PER2 via highly conserved sites that flank the FASP phosphorylation region in the CKBD.
source: The ability of these kinases to phosphorylate lower affinity, non-consensus sites on PER2 is likely dependent on the formation of a stable, stoichiometric complex with PER2 via highly conserved sites that flank the FASP phosphorylation region in the CKBD (Eide et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The generally low activity of CK1 on clock-relevant non-consensus sequences may be important for the slow timescale of circadian rhythms.
source: The generally low activity of CK1 that we observe on clock-relevant non-consensus sequences may also be important for the slow timescale of circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the kinase assay data.

claim: Low kinase activity is conserved in KaiC, the enzyme that controls circadian timing in the cyanobacterial system.
source: This property is also conserved in KaiC, the enzyme that controls circadian timing in the cyanobacterial system (Abe et al., 2015), suggesting commonalities in the biochemical origins of building slow biological clocks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.
